assessment.clarify_core: Onset, duration (>2 weeks?), course (continuous/episodic), pervasiveness (most of day/most days?), context (precipitating stressor vs spontaneous), subjective distress, functional impairment
assessment.screen_for_syndrome: Anhedonia, fatigue/low energy, sleep disturbance (early morning awakening), appetite/weight change, psychomotor change, cognitive symptoms (poor concentration, guilt, hopelessness), suicidal ideation (passive vs active, intent, plan, means)
assessment.rule_out_mimics: Bipolarity: past elevated mood, decreased sleep need, impulsivity. Psychosis: mood-congruent delusions, nihilism, guilt. Anxiety disorders: primary anxiety with secondary sadness. Substance: alcohol, cannabis, sedatives. Medical: hypothyroidism, anemia, chronic pain, neurological illness. Medications: steroids, beta-blockers, isotretinoin
assessment.psychosocial_context: Recent losses, interpersonal conflicts, chronic stressors (caregiving, financial, academic), personality traits (neuroticism, dependency), supports, coping styles
assessment.risk_assessment: Current suicidal ideation, past attempts, hopelessness, command hallucinations, protective factors

differential_diagnosis.primary_psychiatric: Major Depressive Disorder, Persistent Depressive Disorder (Dysthymia), Adjustment Disorder with Depressed Mood, Bipolar Depression, Depressive episode with psychotic features
differential_diagnosis.secondary_mimics: Anxiety disorder (GAD, panic), Substance-induced depressive disorder, Depression due to medical condition, Normal grief vs complicated grief
differential_diagnosis.red_flags: Bipolarity: antidepressant-induced worsening, early onset, episodic course, family history. Psychosis: mood-congruent delusions, catatonia. Suicide: active plan, means, intent

management.immediate_priorities: Ensure safety: assess need for admission if high suicide risk. Address acute stressors. Involve family if appropriate.
management.biological_interventions: First-line antidepressants: SSRIs (sertraline, escitalopram). Start low, go slow; explain delayed onset. Avoid antidepressant monotherapy if bipolarity suspected. Baseline labs if indicated (TSH, CBC).
management.psychological_interventions: Psychoeducation (illness model, treatment expectations). Supportive therapy initially. CBT/IPT once acute distress reduces. Address maladaptive cognitions (guilt, hopelessness).
management.social_interventions: Problem-solving around stressors. Strengthen supports. Occupational/academic accommodations if needed.
management.follow_up_monitoring: Review in 1-2 weeks initially. Monitor suicidality, adherence, side effects. Plan duration (minimum 6-9 months post-remission).

faculty_pearls: Persistent sadness ≠ depression → syndrome first
Always rule out bipolar depression
Risk assessment is more important than diagnosis
Treatment is bio-psycho-social, not just an SSRI

assessment.clarify_core: Onset, duration (>2 weeks), specific areas affected (hobbies, work, relationships, food, sex), any activities that still bring pleasure, associated fatigue/low energy
assessment.screen_for_syndrome: Depressed mood, sleep/appetite changes, fatigue, guilt/worthlessness, concentration difficulties, suicidal ideation. Assess for bipolar depression (episodic pattern). Screen for schizophrenia negative symptoms (avolition, alogia, affective flattening).
assessment.rule_out_mimics: Parkinson's disease (early sign), stroke affecting reward circuits, hypogonadism (low testosterone), hypothyroidism, chronic pain syndromes. Substance: stimulant withdrawal, chronic alcohol use. Medication: antipsychotics (emotional blunting), SSRIs (emotional blunting as side effect).
assessment.psychosocial_context: Burnout, chronic stress, relationship dissatisfaction, career disillusionment, lack of meaningful activities, social isolation, anhedonia as defense mechanism against trauma
assessment.risk_assessment: Anhedonia is strong predictor of suicide - assess ideation, plans, intent. Self-neglect if avolition present.

differential_diagnosis.primary_psychiatric: Major Depressive Disorder (core symptom), Persistent Depressive Disorder, Schizophrenia (negative symptoms), Schizoaffective Disorder, Bipolar Depression, Substance-Induced Depressive Disorder
differential_diagnosis.secondary_mimics: Parkinson's disease (mesolimbic dopamine dysfunction), stroke (reward circuit damage), hypogonadism, hypothyroidism, chronic pain syndrome, medication side effects, normal aging vs pathological anhedonia
differential_diagnosis.red_flags: Complete anhedonia with profound avolition → suggests schizophrenia negative symptoms. Motor slowing → parkinsonism. Sudden onset after neurological event → vascular

management.immediate_priorities: Suicide risk assessment (anhedonia correlates strongly). Address self-care if compromised by avolition. Rule out neurological causes urgently if sudden onset.
management.biological_interventions: Antidepressants: SSRIs, SNRIs. Bupropion (NDRI) for dopaminergic enhancement - often helpful for anhedonia. Dopamine agonists if Parkinson's-related. Rule out: TSH, testosterone, vitamin B12.
management.psychological_interventions: Behavioral activation (gradual re-engagement in pleasurable activities - even without intrinsic motivation initially). CBT for depression. Pleasure mapping to identify any remaining interests. Mindfulness-based approaches.
management.social_interventions: Encourage social engagement even without intrinsic motivation. Structured activities. Support for reintegration into meaningful roles. Family education about behavioral activation.
management.follow_up_monitoring: Monitor return of interest and pleasure as key recovery marker. Adjust antidepressant dose if no response after 4-6 weeks. Bupropion trial if SSRIs ineffective for anhedonia.

faculty_pearls: Anhedonia is often the last symptom to resolve in depression treatment
In schizophrenia, anhedonia is a negative symptom - responds poorly to antipsychotics, requires psychosocial interventions
Bupropion may be particularly helpful due to dopaminergic action
Distinguish 'loss of interest' (motivational) from 'inability to experience pleasure' (consummatory) - latter is more severe and treatment-resistant

assessment.clarify_core: Onset, duration (constant vs fluctuating), content of hopeless thoughts (future, relationships, recovery), worthlessness: guilt, shame, feeling like a burden, intensity of distress, impact on help-seeking
assessment.screen_for_syndrome: Anhedonia, depressed mood, fatigue, sleep/appetite changes, concentration problems, suicidal ideation. Look for rumination patterns, excessive guilt. Screen for BPD (abandonment fears, identity disturbance).
assessment.rule_out_mimics: Hypothyroidism (frontal lobe effects), neurological conditions (stroke affecting frontal circuits), depression due to general medical condition. Substance: alcohol intoxication/withdrawal, stimulant crash, cannabis. Medication: corticosteroids, interferon-alpha.
assessment.psychosocial_context: Recent failures/rejections, chronic adversity, trauma history, cultural/religious beliefs about self-worth, family dynamics (critical vs supportive), socioeconomic challenges, unrealistic self-expectations, perfectionism
assessment.risk_assessment: Hopelessness is strongest predictor of suicide - assess ideation, plans, intent, means, past attempts, protective factors, access to means. More dangerous than depression without hopelessness.

differential_diagnosis.primary_psychiatric: Major Depressive Disorder, Persistent Depressive Disorder, Bipolar Depression, Adjustment Disorder with Depressed Mood, Borderline Personality Disorder, Schizoaffective Disorder (depressive type)
differential_diagnosis.secondary_mimics: Hypothyroidism, neurological conditions (frontal/temporal lesions), medication side effects, grief/bereavement (transient), situational stress without disorder, demoralization
differential_diagnosis.red_flags: Psychotic depression (mood-congruent delusions of worthlessness: 'I deserve punishment', 'I am evil'). Catatonia (mutism, negativism). Severe hopelessness with active suicide plan → emergency

management.immediate_priorities: Urgent suicide risk assessment. If high risk: close monitoring, remove means, emergency evaluation, consider involuntary hospitalization if imminent danger. Address acute crises.
management.biological_interventions: SSRIs first-line. ECT for severe depression with psychotic features OR high suicide risk OR treatment resistance. Rule out: TSH, electrolytes. Consider augmentation strategies if partial response.
management.psychological_interventions: CBT (challenging cognitive distortions about hopelessness/worthlessness). Behavioral activation to build mastery and hope. DBT emotion regulation skills. Address maladaptive core beliefs.
management.social_interventions: Strengthen support systems, address real-life stressors, involve family in safety planning, meaningful activity engagement, address cultural/religious factors.
management.follow_up_monitoring: Frequent contact initially (weekly or more). Monitor suicide risk very closely. Reassess hopelessness as treatment progresses - improving hope is good prognostic sign. Consider ECT if no rapid improvement.

faculty_pearls: Hopelessness is the single strongest predictor of suicide - more than depression severity itself
In depressive disorders, worthlessness is often accompanied by excessive guilt - distinguish from realistic regret
ECT is underutilized for high-risk depression - can be lifesaving
Cultural factors influence expression - some cultures express through somatic complaints rather than verbal statements of worthlessness

assessment.clarify_core: Onset, triggers (spontaneous vs minor vs major), frequency (daily/weekly), duration (brief vs prolonged), context (home only vs public situations), ability to control/suppress, associated mood state
assessment.screen_for_syndrome: Depressed mood, anhedonia, fatigue, appetite/sleep changes, guilt, suicidal ideation. Also screen for anxiety disorders, PTSD, adjustment disorder, PMDD (timing with menstrual cycle). BPD screening (affective lability, abandonment fears).
assessment.rule_out_mimics: Pseudobulbar affect (stroke, ALS, MS - inappropriate laughing/crying not matching mood). Hormonal: pregnancy, postpartum, menopause, thyroid dysfunction. Substance: alcohol intoxication/withdrawal. Medication: SSRIs (emotional lability as paradoxical effect).
assessment.psychosocial_context: Recent losses, trauma, high stress, relationship conflicts, lack of emotional support, cultural attitudes about crying (stigma vs acceptance), personality factors (emotionality, alexithymia)
assessment.risk_assessment: Assess for suicidal ideation - frequent crying can indicate severe distress. Evaluate for self-harm behaviors. Impact on functioning (work absences, social withdrawal, driving).

differential_diagnosis.primary_psychiatric: Major Depressive Disorder, Persistent Depressive Disorder, Bipolar Depression or Mixed Episode, Adjustment Disorder, PTSD, Grief/Bereavement, Borderline Personality Disorder, Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder
differential_diagnosis.secondary_mimics: Pseudobulbar affect (neurological disorder), hormonal changes (pregnancy, postpartum, menopause, thyroid), medication side effects, substance effects, normal emotional expression
differential_diagnosis.red_flags: Pseudobulbar affect (inappropriate, uncontrollable crying not matching mood - suggests neurological). Severe suicidal ideation with frequent crying. Sudden onset in middle-aged/elderly (consider stroke)

management.immediate_priorities: Assess for acute suicide risk. Support patient during distress. Normalize emotional expression while addressing underlying cause.
management.biological_interventions: Antidepressants for underlying depression/anxiety. Hormone evaluation if indicated (FSH, LH, TSH). For pseudobulbar affect: dextromethorphan/quinidine, SSRIs, TCAs.
management.psychological_interventions: CBT to address underlying depression/anxiety. DBT emotion regulation skills (mindfulness, distress tolerance). Grief counseling if appropriate. Stress management techniques. Emotional awareness training.
management.social_interventions: Supportive environment, psychoeducation about emotional expression, address triggering situations, strengthen support network, family education about validating emotions.
management.follow_up_monitoring: Monitor frequency and triggers of crying spells. Improvement in emotional regulation indicates treatment response. Monitor for pseudobulbar response to treatment.

faculty_pearls: Frequent crying spells can be the presenting symptom of depression even without overt sadness reported
Distinguish crying as symptom vs appropriate grief - context, triggers, pervasiveness help differentiate
Pseudobulbar affect presents with uncontrollable laughing or crying incongruent with mood - think neurological, not psychiatric
Some cultures express distress through somatic symptoms rather than crying - cultural formulation essential

assessment.clarify_core: Onset (gradual vs sudden), pattern (morning fatigue vs evening, worse with activity vs constant), rest improvement (does rest help?), sleep quantity/quality, impact on work/social/self-care
assessment.screen_for_syndrome: Depressed mood, anhedonia, sleep/appetite changes, guilt, concentration problems. Also consider anxiety, mania/hypomania (during crash), medical causes. Screen for somatization disorder.
assessment.rule_out_mimics: Anemia (CBC), hypothyroidism (TSH), diabetes (HbA1c), heart failure, sleep apnea (overnight study), chronic fatigue syndrome, fibromyalgia, infections (mononucleosis, EBV, COVID), malignancy. Substance: alcohol, sedatives, stimulant withdrawal. Medication: antihistamines, beta-blockers, antidepressants (fatigue as side effect).
assessment.psychosocial_context: Chronic stress, burnout, lack of meaningful activity, poor sleep hygiene, relationship conflicts, work demands, physical inactivity, poor nutrition, caffeine dependence/withdrawal, caregiver fatigue
assessment.risk_assessment: Safety - severe fatigue can impair driving, work safety. Evaluate for associated suicidal ideation if depression present. Risk of self-neglect.

differential_diagnosis.primary_psychiatric: Major Depressive Disorder, Bipolar Depression, Persistent Depressive Disorder, Adjustment Disorder, Somatic Symptom Disorder, Depressive disorder due to another medical condition
differential_diagnosis.secondary_mimics: Anemia, hypothyroidism, diabetes, heart failure, sleep apnea, chronic fatigue syndrome, fibromyalgia, viral infections, malignancy, medication side effects, substance use/withdrawal
differential_diagnosis.red_flags: Rapid onset fatigue with neurological symptoms → stroke, encephalitis, meningitis. Fatigue with weight loss + night sweats → malignancy. Severe orthostatic symptoms → endocrine/cardiac. Fatigue with jaundice → hepatic

management.immediate_priorities: Rule out urgent medical causes. Address safety concerns if fatigue impairs functioning significantly (driving, operating machinery).
management.biological_interventions: Basic labs: CBC, TSH, BMP, HbA1c, vitamin B12, folate, iron studies. Treat identified causes. Antidepressants if depression present. Sleep study if OSA suspected (snoring, witnessed apneas, daytime sleepiness).
management.psychological_interventions: CBT for depression and chronic fatigue. Sleep hygiene education. Activity pacing (for CFS - avoid boom-bust cycle). Stress management. Behavioral activation. Address illness beliefs.
management.social_interventions: Address work accommodations if needed. Graded activity programs. Support groups (for CFS, fibromyalgia). Family education. Address caregiver burden if present.
management.follow_up_monitoring: Reassess fatigue levels regularly. Monitor antidepressant response if prescribed. Re-evaluate if fatigue persists despite treatment - consider specialist referral (neurology, endocrinology, sleep medicine).

faculty_pearls: Fatigue is one of the most common and nonspecific symptoms - requires thorough medical + psychiatric evaluation
Depression-related fatigue is often worse in morning and improves with activity, whereas medical fatigue often worsens with exertion
In depression, fatigue is present despite adequate sleep - distinguish from sleep deprivation
Chronic Fatigue Syndrome requires fatigue lasting 6+ months, not explained by medical/psychiatric causes, with post-exertional malaise

assessment.clarify_core: Onset (sudden vs gradual), duration (days/weeks), intensity (normal happiness vs abnormal euphoria), consistency (all day vs fluctuating), context (triggers vs spontaneous), insight (does patient recognize mood change?), functional impact (productivity vs impairment)
assessment.screen_for_syndrome: Decreased need for sleep (core feature - feels rested), increased activity, racing thoughts, grandiosity, distractibility, risk-taking behaviors (spending, sex, driving). Also screen for hypomania criteria. Assess for psychotic features (mood-congruent delusions).
assessment.rule_out_mimics: Hyperthyroidism (TSH, T3, T4 - weight loss, tremor, heat intolerance), Cushing's syndrome, neurological conditions (stroke, tumor, epilepsy - mania can be ictal or postictal). Substance: stimulants (cocaine, amphetamines, meth), MDMA, cannabis, alcohol intoxication. Medication: corticosteroids, dopaminergic agents (levodopa, pramipexole), antidepressants (switch to mania).
assessment.psychosocial_context: Recent successes, mania triggers (sleep deprivation, substance use, schedule disruption), stress (can trigger or exacerbate), circadian disruption, seasonal patterns (spring/summer for mania).
assessment.risk_assessment: Dangerous behaviors: reckless spending, sexual promiscuity, risky investments, dangerous driving, physical risk-taking. Harm to self or others. Insight and judgment. Impulsivity. Access to resources (credit cards, vehicles).

differential_diagnosis.primary_psychiatric: Bipolar I Disorder (manic episode), Bipolar II Disorder (hypomanic episode), Cyclothymic Disorder, Schizoaffective Disorder (bipolar type), Substance/Medication-Induced Bipolar Disorder
differential_diagnosis.secondary_mimics: Hyperthyroidism, Cushing's syndrome, stimulant intoxication, steroid-induced euphoria, neurological conditions (temporal lobe epilepsy, stroke, tumor), normal happiness/celebration, personality traits (cheerful temperament, hyperthymic personality)
differential_diagnosis.red_flags: Psychotic features with mood incongruence → consider schizoaffective or primary psychosis. Rapid mood lability (hours) → borderline personality. Severe disinhibition with legal consequences. Catatonia. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (if on antipsychotics)

management.immediate_priorities: Safety assessment for risky behaviors. If manic with poor insight: consider involuntary hospitalization. Remove access to money/credit if spending dangerously. Protect from sexual exploitation. Supervise driving.
management.biological_interventions: Mood stabilizers: lithium (first-line for mania), valproate, carbamazepine, lamotrigine. Antipsychotics: olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone, aripiprazole (all have evidence for mania). Benzodiazepines for acute agitation (lorazepam, clonazepam). Rule out: TSH.
management.psychological_interventions: Psychoeducation about bipolar disorder (chronic, relapsing, needs ongoing treatment). Adherence counseling. Cognitive therapy for insight (when mood stable). Family-focused therapy to improve communication and early detection. Relapse prevention planning.
management.social_interventions: Limit access to financial resources during acute episode. Supervise high-risk activities. Involve family in safety monitoring. Structured environment. Regular sleep schedule.
management.follow_up_monitoring: Frequent monitoring initially (daily to weekly). Monitor for medication side effects. Monitor mood, sleep, activity, risk behaviors. Long-term maintenance treatment required (lifelong for most). Monitor lithium/valproate levels.

faculty_pearls: Screen carefully for bipolar disorder before prescribing antidepressants - antidepressants can precipitate mania in undiagnosed bipolar patients
Elevated mood with psychotic features (delusions of grandeur, special powers) suggests severe mania requiring aggressive treatment with antipsychotics + mood stabilizers
Distinguish mania from normal happiness: mania is pervasive, associated with functional impairment, and accompanied by other symptoms (decreased sleep need, increased activity)
Lack of insight is characteristic of mania - patient may not recognize mood change and may resist treatment - family input crucial

assessment.clarify_core: Onset, triggers (specific situations/people vs generalized), frequency (constant vs episodic), intensity (mild annoyance vs rage episodes), duration of episodes, expression (verbal, physical, suppressed), impact (relationships, work, legal consequences)
assessment.screen_for_syndrome: Depressed mood, anhedonia, sleep/appetite changes, concentration problems. Also consider mania/hypomania (if episodic with elevated mood), PTSD (hyperarousal), ADHD (lifelong pattern), personality disorders (BPD, antisocial, intermittent explosive). Look for associated: anxiety, impulsivity, sleep disturbances.
assessment.rule_out_mimics: Hyperthyroidism (irritability, heat intolerance, weight loss, tremor), hypoglycemia (episodic irritability with hunger), PMS/PMDD (timing with cycle), neurological conditions (temporal lobe epilepsy), chronic pain. Substance: alcohol withdrawal, stimulant intoxication/withdrawal, steroid use, caffeine excess. Medication: steroids, SSRIs (activation syndrome), stimulants (for ADHD - rebound irritability).
assessment.psychosocial_context: Chronic stress, relationship conflicts, work pressure, sleep deprivation, recent losses, trauma history, learned patterns of anger expression, family dynamics (aggressive vs validating), cultural factors around anger expression
assessment.risk_assessment: Aggression risk: history of violence, access to weapons, threats made, recent substance use, history of assaults. Domestic violence risk (perpetrator or victim). Self-harm during rage episodes. Suicidal ideation in context of BPD or depression.

differential_diagnosis.primary_psychiatric: Major Depressive Disorder (especially in children/adolescents), Bipolar Disorder (manic or mixed episodes), Generalized Anxiety Disorder, PTSD, Intermittent Explosive Disorder, Borderline Personality Disorder, ADHD, Disruptive Mood Dysregulation Disorder (children)
differential_diagnosis.secondary_mimics: Hyperthyroidism, hypoglycemia, PMS/PMDD, neurological conditions, chronic pain, substance intoxication/withdrawal, medication side effects, normal stress response
differential_diagnosis.red_flags: History of violence, weapon access, threats of harm, severe rage episodes with amnesia, physical aggression resulting in injury, domestic violence, legal consequences of aggression

management.immediate_priorities: Assess for imminent violence risk. If high risk: safety planning, remove weapons, consider hospitalization. Address any acute crises. Assess for self-harm/suicide risk.
management.biological_interventions: Treat underlying disorder: antidepressants for depression/anxiety, mood stabilizers for bipolar/IED, stimulants for ADHD. For IED: SSRIs, mood stabilizers, antipsychotics. Rule out: TSH, glucose, electrolytes.
management.psychological_interventions: CBT for anger management (cognitive restructuring, anger triggers, coping skills). DBT skills (emotion regulation, distress tolerance, interpersonal effectiveness). Conflict resolution skills. Stress management. Relaxation techniques.
management.social_interventions: Address environmental triggers. Family therapy for communication patterns. Anger management groups. Workplace interventions if work-related. Address substance use.
management.follow_up_monitoring: Monitor frequency and intensity of irritability episodes. Assess for response to treatment. Monitor for aggression/violence. Re-evaluate if no improvement.

faculty_pearls: In children and adolescents, irritability is often the primary presenting symptom of depression rather than sadness - don't miss depression
Irritability in context of elevated mood suggests mania or mixed episode rather than depression
Chronic irritability with mood lability and interpersonal difficulties is characteristic of borderline personality disorder - think DBT
Differentiate irritable mood from anger attacks - the latter are discrete episodes with autonomic activation (tachycardia, flushing) and may indicate Intermittent Explosive Disorder

assessment.clarify_core: Onset: When did increased activity/goal-directed behavior begin? Duration: How long has it persisted? Frequency/Pervasiveness: How often does it occur? Context: Any triggers or situations? Functional impact: How does it affect daily life?
assessment.screen_for_syndrome: Screen for associated psychiatric symptoms relevant to Increased Activity/Goal-Directed Behavior. Consider mood, anxiety, psychotic, cognitive, and behavioral symptoms. Assess for syndromic presentations.
assessment.rule_out_mimics: Medical: Consider relevant medical conditions based on symptom presentation. Substance: Assess for alcohol, stimulant, sedative, cannabis, hallucinogen use or withdrawal. Medication: Review current medications for potential side effects.
assessment.psychosocial_context: Recent life events, chronic stressors, relationship dynamics, work/school environment, trauma history, social support systems, cultural factors, sleep patterns.
assessment.risk_assessment: Assess for immediate safety concerns related to Increased Activity/Goal-Directed Behavior. Evaluate for self-harm, suicide risk, risk to others. Consider impact on judgment and safety-critical activities.

differential_diagnosis.secondary_mimics: Medical conditions, substance use/withdrawal, medication side effects, neurological conditions, endocrine disorders, normal variations.
differential_diagnosis.red_flags: Symptoms suggesting medical emergency, severe psychiatric decompensation, acute danger to self/others, rapid symptom progression, atypical presentations.

management.immediate_priorities: Safety assessment and stabilization. Address any acute crises or emergencies. Rule out urgent medical causes. Initiate appropriate interventions based on severity.
management.biological_interventions: Consider medications based on underlying diagnosis. Complete relevant medical investigations. Treat any identified medical causes. Monitor medication response and side effects.
management.psychological_interventions: Implement evidence-based psychotherapies appropriate to diagnosis. Provide psychoeducation about symptoms and treatment. Teach coping strategies and skills.
management.social_interventions: Address psychosocial stressors and environmental factors. Engage support systems. Consider accommodations in work/school. Address social determinants impacting recovery.
management.follow_up_monitoring: Regular monitoring of symptom severity and treatment response. Use standardized measures when appropriate. Adjust treatment based on response. Long-term management planning.

faculty_pearls: Consider Increased Activity/Goal-Directed Behavior within the broader clinical context - isolated symptoms may be less diagnostically significant than symptom clusters.
Cultural factors significantly influence symptom expression and help-seeking - cultural formulation is essential.
Screening for comorbid conditions is important - psychiatric disorders frequently co-occur.
Patient education about the symptom and its treatment improves engagement and outcomes.

assessment.clarify_core: Onset: When did rapid mood swings begin? Duration: How long has it persisted? Frequency/Pervasiveness: How often does it occur? Context: Any triggers or situations? Functional impact: How does it affect daily life?
assessment.screen_for_syndrome: Screen for associated psychiatric symptoms relevant to Rapid Mood Swings. Consider mood, anxiety, psychotic, cognitive, and behavioral symptoms. Assess for syndromic presentations.
assessment.rule_out_mimics: Medical: Consider relevant medical conditions based on symptom presentation. Substance: Assess for alcohol, stimulant, sedative, cannabis, hallucinogen use or withdrawal. Medication: Review current medications for potential side effects.
assessment.psychosocial_context: Recent life events, chronic stressors, relationship dynamics, work/school environment, trauma history, social support systems, cultural factors, sleep patterns.
assessment.risk_assessment: Assess for immediate safety concerns related to Rapid Mood Swings. Evaluate for self-harm, suicide risk, risk to others. Consider impact on judgment and safety-critical activities.

differential_diagnosis.primary_psychiatric: Consider primary psychiatric disorders where this symptom is a core or associated feature based on diagnostic criteria and clinical presentation.
differential_diagnosis.secondary_mimics: Medical conditions, substance use/withdrawal, medication side effects, neurological conditions, endocrine disorders, normal variations.
differential_diagnosis.red_flags: Symptoms suggesting medical emergency, severe psychiatric decompensation, acute danger to self/others, rapid symptom progression, atypical presentations.

management.immediate_priorities: Safety assessment and stabilization. Address any acute crises or emergencies. Rule out urgent medical causes. Initiate appropriate interventions based on severity.
management.biological_interventions: Consider medications based on underlying diagnosis. Complete relevant medical investigations. Treat any identified medical causes. Monitor medication response and side effects.
management.psychological_interventions: Implement evidence-based psychotherapies appropriate to diagnosis. Provide psychoeducation about symptoms and treatment. Teach coping strategies and skills.
management.social_interventions: Address psychosocial stressors and environmental factors. Engage support systems. Consider accommodations in work/school. Address social determinants impacting recovery.
management.follow_up_monitoring: Regular monitoring of symptom severity and treatment response. Use standardized measures when appropriate. Adjust treatment based on response. Long-term management planning.

faculty_pearls: Consider Rapid Mood Swings within the broader clinical context - isolated symptoms may be less diagnostically significant than symptom clusters.
Cultural factors significantly influence symptom expression and help-seeking - cultural formulation is essential.
Screening for comorbid conditions is important - psychiatric disorders frequently co-occur.
Patient education about the symptom and its treatment improves engagement and outcomes.

assessment.clarify_core: Duration (>6 months?), frequency (most days?), topics (multiple areas: health, finances, relationships, work) or single focus, control difficulty (can stop/redirect worry?), physical symptoms (tension, restlessness, fatigue, muscle aches, sleep disturbance)
assessment.screen_for_syndrome: Depressive symptoms (low mood, anhedonia, suicidal thoughts). Panic attacks. OCD (obsessions as worry). PTSD (worry about future harm). Health anxiety. Substance use to manage worry.
assessment.rule_out_mimics: Hyperthyroidism (TSH, tachycardia, weight loss, tremor), cardiac arrhythmias (ECG), pheochromocytoma (episodic HTN, headaches, sweating), hypoglycemia (diabetic, relieved by food). Substance: caffeine excess, stimulant use, alcohol withdrawal, cannabis. Medication: sympathomimetics, steroids, some antidepressants (activation).
assessment.psychosocial_context: Chronic stressors, recent life changes (job, bereavement, relocation), family anxiety history, learned worry patterns (catastrophizing, intolerance of uncertainty), perfectionism, trauma history, cultural factors
assessment.risk_assessment: Associated depression and suicide risk. Functional impairment: work, relationships, self-care. Substance use to manage worry (benzodiazepines, alcohol). Sleep deprivation from worry.

differential_diagnosis.primary_psychiatric: Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD), Adjustment Disorder with Anxiety, Panic Disorder, OCD (worry as obsession), Depressive Disorder with anxious distress, PTSD (future-oriented worry), Illness Anxiety Disorder
differential_diagnosis.secondary_mimics: Hyperthyroidism, cardiac arrhythmias, pheochromocytoma, hypoglycemia, caffeine excess, stimulant effects, normal stress response, medical illness anxiety (organic disease)
differential_diagnosis.red_flags: Severe depression with suicidal ideation, panic attacks with agoraphobia, substance dependence, marked functional impairment, psychotic symptoms (worry about delusional content), autonomic hyperactivity suggesting medical cause

management.immediate_priorities: Assess for depression and suicide risk. Address any acute crises. Screen for substance use to manage anxiety (benzodiazepines, alcohol).
management.biological_interventions: SSRIs first-line: sertraline, escitalopram, paroxetine (start low, titrate over 2-4 weeks). SNRIs: venlafaxine XR, duloxetine. Buspirone (non-addictive, no sexual side effects). Short-term benzos for acute symptoms only (cautious, 2-4 weeks max). Rule out: TSH, ECG if cardiac symptoms.
management.psychological_interventions: CBT for GAD (cognitive restructuring, worry exposure/triggering, problem-solving skills, relaxation training). Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction. Acceptance and Commitment Therapy. Psychoeducation about anxiety (fight-flight-freeze, physiology).
management.social_interventions: Stress management (time management, prioritization). Lifestyle modifications (regular exercise, sleep hygiene, limit caffeine/alcohol). Address chronic stressors. Family education about anxiety disorders. Support groups.
management.follow_up_monitoring: Monitor with GAD-7 scale. Antidepressant response takes 4-6 weeks - manage expectations. Monitor for benzo dependence if prescribed. Regular follow-up initially (2-4 weeks). Minimum 6-12 months treatment.

faculty_pearls: GAD worry is excessive, difficult to control, and associated with multiple physical symptoms - distinguish from normal stress
Patients with GAD often 'worry about worrying' (meta-worry) - this is a key target in CBT
Screen for depression - comorbid depression is common (up to 60%) and requires combined treatment approach
Physical exercise is an evidence-based adjunctive treatment for GAD - often underutilized but effective as monotherapy for mild cases

assessment.clarify_core: Onset of first attack, frequency (how often?), duration (typically 10-30 min, max 1 hour), triggers (specific situations/cues or unexpected/unexpected), symptoms: palpitations, sweating, trembling, shortness of breath, choking sensation, chest pain, nausea, dizziness, derealization/depersonalization, fear of dying/losing control/going crazy, chills/hot flushes
assessment.screen_for_syndrome: Screen for Panic Disorder: recurrent unexpected attacks, worry about future attacks for ≥1 month, maladaptive behavior change (avoidance). Also screen for agoraphobia (fear of situations where escape difficult). Depression, substance use (benzodiazepines, alcohol).
assessment.rule_out_mimics: Cardiac conditions: arrhythmias, myocardial infarction (chest pain, ECG changes, cardiac enzymes), MVP. Pulmonary: asthma, PE, pulmonary embolus. Thyroid: hyperthyroidism. Neurological: seizure (post-ictal anxiety), TIA. Hypoglycemia (diabetic). Substance: caffeine, stimulants, cannabis, alcohol withdrawal. Medication: sympathomimetics, steroids, some antidepressants.
assessment.psychosocial_context: Recent stressors, trauma history (can trigger), family anxiety history, learned fear responses (classical conditioning), catastrophic thinking patterns, interoceptive conditioning (fear of bodily sensations), avoidance learning
assessment.risk_assessment: Associated depression and suicide risk. Agoraphobia: avoidance driving work/school, leaving home. Substance use to prevent/manage attacks (benzodiazepines, alcohol). Dangerous situations during attacks: driving, operating machinery, heights, water.

differential_diagnosis.primary_psychiatric: Panic Disorder with or without Agoraphobia, Other Specified Anxiety Disorder, Substance-Induced Anxiety Disorder, PTSD (panic attacks as symptom), Social Anxiety Disorder (situation-specific)
differential_diagnosis.secondary_mimics: Cardiac arrhythmias (SVT, atrial fibrillation), myocardial infarction, asthma, pulmonary embolism, hyperthyroidism, seizures (temporal lobe), hypoglycemia, pheochromocytoma, vestibular disorders, medication side effects
differential_diagnosis.red_flags: Chest pain with cardiac risk factors (age, hypertension, diabetes, smoking, family history) → rule out MI first. Shortness of breath with respiratory disease/PE risk. Neurological deficits (focal weakness, speech changes). Loss of consciousness. Persistent symptoms beyond panic attack duration

management.immediate_priorities: Rule out medical emergencies (cardiac, pulmonary) first - don't assume anxiety. Safety during attacks - avoid driving if frequent. Assess depression/suicide risk. Address substance use (benzo, alcohol).
management.biological_interventions: SSRIs first-line: sertraline, paroxetine, escitalopram (effective for panic, prevent anticipatory anxiety). SNRIs: venlafaxine XR. Short-term benzos (alprazolam, clonazepam) for acute symptom control - use sparingly, 2-4 weeks. Rule out: ECG, TSH, CXR if respiratory symptoms.
management.psychological_interventions: CBT for panic (psychoeducation about panic physiology - 'fight or flight', interoceptive exposure - deliberately inducing symptoms to extinguish fear, cognitive restructuring of catastrophic beliefs, breathing retraining). Panic control techniques for acute attacks. Gradual exposure to avoided situations (in vivo).
management.social_interventions: Gradual exposure to avoided situations with support person. Family education about panic disorder (not 'crazy', treatable). Support for agoraphobia recovery. Address substance dependence.
management.follow_up_monitoring: Monitor attack frequency and severity. Antidepressant response 4-6 weeks - start before titrating benzos down. Taper benzos once CBT effective - risk of dependence. Regular follow-up. Minimum 6-12 months treatment.

faculty_pearls: Always consider cardiac causes first in patients with chest pain and panic symptoms - don't attribute to anxiety prematurely, especially in older patients or cardiac risk factors
Interoceptive exposure (deliberately inducing physical sensations: hyperventilation, spinning, etc.) is key CBT technique for panic - patients learn sensations aren't dangerous
Patients often develop avoidance (agoraphobia) - early intervention prevents disability, treat both panic and avoidance
Benzodiazepine dependence risk high in panic disorder - use short-term with clear plan to taper once CBT/SSRIs effective

assessment.clarify_core: Onset, frequency, duration, precipitating factors (exercise, stress, rest, position), associated symptoms: chest pain, sweating, dizziness, syncope, anxiety/fear, triggers (thoughts, situations, spontaneous)
assessment.screen_for_syndrome: Panic disorder (with other panic symptoms). Anxiety disorders (GAD, social anxiety). Depression. Cardiac risk factors assessment. Respiratory history. Substance use (stimulants, nicotine, caffeine, alcohol withdrawal).
assessment.rule_out_mimics: Cardiac: arrhythmias (PSVT, AFib, VT), MI, MVP, cardiomyopathy. Pulmonary: asthma, COPD, PE, pneumothorax. Thyroid: hyperthyroidism. Anemia (tachycardia, breathlessness on exertion). Substance: caffeine, stimulants, nicotine, alcohol withdrawal. Medication: beta-agonists, theophylline, sympathomimetics.
assessment.psychosocial_context: Anxiety-provoking situations (social, work, health), catastrophic health beliefs, interoceptive hypersensitivity, trauma history (medical trauma), health anxiety.
assessment.risk_assessment: Cardiac emergency risk (chest pain with red flags). Respiratory emergency. Anxiety-driven self-harm. Driving safety if symptomatic.

differential_diagnosis.primary_psychiatric: Panic Disorder, GAD, Social Anxiety Disorder, Illness Anxiety Disorder, Depression with somatic symptoms, Somatic Symptom Disorder
differential_diagnosis.secondary_mimics: Cardiac arrhythmias, myocardial infarction, asthma, COPD, pulmonary embolism, hyperthyroidism, anemia, deconditioning, medication side effects
differential_diagnosis.red_flags: Chest pain with radiation, diaphoresis, nausea, cardiac risk factors → rule out MI. Sudden severe breathlessness with pleuritic pain → PE. Syncope, arrhythmia on ECG. Wheezing, past asthma/COPD → respiratory cause

management.immediate_priorities: Rule out cardiac/pulmonary emergencies first. ECG, CXR, cardiac enzymes if indicated. Safety - avoid driving if symptomatic.
management.biological_interventions: Treat underlying anxiety/panic: SSRIs, SNRIs. Beta-blockers (propranolol) for performance anxiety or situational - helps with physical symptoms. Benzos short-term for acute. Treat medical causes: antiarrhythmics, bronchodilators, antithyroid if hyperthyroidism.
management.psychological_interventions: CBT for anxiety/panic. Interoceptive exposure. Breathing retraining. Cognitive restructuring of health beliefs. Relaxation techniques.
management.social_interventions: Address anxiety-provoking situations. Gradual exposure. Family support. Lifestyle: limit caffeine/stimulants.
management.follow_up_monitoring: Monitor frequency of symptoms. Cardiac/pulmonary follow-up if medical cause. Monitor anxiety treatment response.

faculty_pearls: Palpitations and breathlessness are somatic symptoms that can be psychiatric or medical - always rule out organic causes first, especially cardiac
Beta-blockers (propranolol) are particularly helpful for performance anxiety - reduce somatic symptoms without sedation
Interoceptive exposure is key for anxiety-driven palpitations - learning that heart racing isn't dangerous
Consider asthma or COPD in patients with breathlessness and anxiety - anxiety can exacerbate respiratory symptoms creating cycle

assessment.clarify_core: Context (during panic attack vs chronic fear), duration, frequency, triggers (situations, thoughts, physical sensations), associated symptoms (palpitations, breathlessness, derealization), impact on behavior (avoidance, safety-seeking, checking)
assessment.screen_for_syndrome: Panic disorder (fear of dying/going crazy is classic). Depression with hopelessness. Psychosis (delusions of dying, persecution). PTSD (fear of harm, flashbacks). OCD (death contamination fears). Health anxiety.
assessment.rule_out_mimics: Cardiac: arrhythmias, MI (can cause fear of dying during event). Neurological: TIA/stroke (fear during event). Respiratory: severe asthma/PE (air hunger). Hypoglycemia (confusion, fear). Substance: hallucinogens (bad trips), stimulants, cannabis. Delirium.
assessment.psychosocial_context: Trauma history (medical trauma, witnessed death), catastrophic thinking, health anxiety, religious/spiritual beliefs about death, previous panic attacks conditioning fear, family history of anxiety
assessment.risk_assessment: Panic-driven dangerous behavior (fleeing, reckless driving). Suicide risk if hopelessness present. Self-harm. Medical avoidance (not seeking help due to fear).

differential_diagnosis.primary_psychiatric: Panic Disorder, GAD, Illness Anxiety Disorder, PTSD, OCD (death-related obsessions), Depression with suicidal thoughts, Specific Phobia (death, illness)
differential_diagnosis.secondary_mimics: Medical emergencies (MI, PE, severe asthma, hypoglycemia), substance effects, delirium, medication side effects, normal fear response
differential_diagnosis.red_flags: Psychotic features (delusions of death, voices commanding death). Catatonia. Severe depression with active suicide plan. Medical emergency (acute cardiac/pulmonary event)

management.immediate_priorities: Rule out medical emergency if fear during physical symptoms. Assess suicide risk if hopelessness present. Address panic attack.
management.biological_interventions: Treat underlying: SSRIs for panic/anxiety. Antipsychotics if psychosis. Treat medical causes. Rule out delirium.
management.psychological_interventions: CBT for panic (psychoeducation, cognitive restructuring of death/control fears). Exposure therapy. Mindfulness. PTSD processing if trauma-related.
management.social_interventions: Safety during panic. Education about panic physiology. Family support. Address avoidance.
management.follow_up_monitoring: Monitor frequency and intensity. Assess treatment response. Monitor suicide risk.

faculty_pearls: Fear of dying/going crazy is classic panic attack symptom - reassure patients about panic physiology
Rule out medical emergencies first if fear occurs with physical symptoms - don't dismiss as anxiety
Catastrophic health beliefs maintain fear - CBT cognitive restructuring essential
In OCD, death fears are obsessions (intrusive, ego-dystonic) unlike panic (acute, spontaneous)

assessment.clarify_core: Onset, specific situations avoided (social, specific phobias, panic triggers, trauma reminders), extent of avoidance (mild inconvenience to severe disability), insight into avoidance, impact on functioning (work, school, relationships), coping strategies used
assessment.screen_for_syndrome: Panic disorder with agoraphobia. Social anxiety disorder. Specific phobias. PTSD (avoidance of trauma reminders). OCD (avoidance of contamination). GAD (situational avoidance). Depression (withdrawal).
assessment.rule_out_mimics: Medical limitations (mobility issues, pain, fatigue). Neurological conditions. Sensory deficits. Cognitive impairment (dementia).
assessment.psychosocial_context: Trauma history, negative experiences (humiliation, bullying), family modeling of avoidance, catastrophic expectations, learned helplessness, low self-efficacy, cultural factors
assessment.risk_assessment: Functional impairment (work, education, social isolation). Safety risks (driving, dangerous situations while anxious). Depression secondary to isolation. Self-neglect.

differential_diagnosis.primary_psychiatric: Agoraphobia (with or without panic), Social Anxiety Disorder, Specific Phobias, PTSD, OCD, GAD, Adjustment Disorder with Avoidance, Autism Spectrum (social avoidance)
differential_diagnosis.secondary_mimics: Medical disabilities, chronic pain, fatigue syndromes, neurological conditions, sensory impairments, cognitive impairment
differential_diagnosis.red_flags: Severe social isolation with depression. Complete inability to leave home for prolonged period. Suicidal ideation with hopelessness. Self-neglect.

management.immediate_priorities: Assess functional impairment. Address depression if present. Evaluate for medical causes of inability to participate.
management.biological_interventions: SSRIs for anxiety disorders. Beta-blockers for performance anxiety. Treat underlying depression. Rule out medical causes.
management.psychological_interventions: Exposure therapy (graded, systematic, in vivo). CBT for anxiety. Social skills training for social anxiety. PTSD processing if applicable.
management.social_interventions: Gradual exposure support. Family education. Address environmental barriers. Support groups. Vocational/educational accommodations.
management.follow_up_monitoring: Monitor reduction in avoidance. Functional improvement. Assess treatment response.

faculty_pearls: Avoidance maintains anxiety through negative reinforcement - exposure is essential treatment
Graded exposure (starting with least feared, gradually increasing) is most effective approach
Functional impairment from avoidance is often greater impairment than anxiety symptoms themselves
Agoraphobia can develop secondary to panic attacks - treat both panic and avoidance

assessment.clarify_core: Specific feared situations (social: performance, interaction, scrutiny; specific: animals, heights, blood, injections, enclosed spaces), duration (>6 months for specific, >6 months for social), anticipatory anxiety, physical symptoms when exposed, avoidance behavior, impact on functioning, insight (recognizes fear excessive?)
assessment.screen_for_syndrome: Other anxiety disorders (panic, GAD, OCD). Depression (secondary to avoidance). Autism spectrum (social difficulties). Substance use to manage situations.
assessment.rule_out_mimics: Medical conditions (mobility issues, pain, respiratory conditions making certain situations dangerous). Neurological conditions. Sensory deficits.
assessment.psychosocial_context: Traumatic experiences with feared object/situation. Learning history (classical conditioning). Family modeling (parent with same phobia). Cultural factors. Social skills deficits.
assessment.risk_assessment: Functional impairment (education, career missed). Social isolation. Depression. Substance use. Dangerous situations (avoiding medical care, driving).

differential_diagnosis.primary_psychiatric: Specific Phobia, Social Anxiety Disorder, Agoraphobia, OCD (phobic avoidance), PTSD (avoidance of trauma cues), Autism Spectrum Disorder (social difficulties)
differential_diagnosis.secondary_mimics: Medical conditions causing limitations, sensory impairments, neurological conditions, normal fear responses (developmentally appropriate)
differential_diagnosis.red_flags: Complete social isolation with depression. Refusal of essential medical care due to phobia (blood, injections). Severe functional impairment. Suicidal ideation.

management.immediate_priorities: Assess functional impairment. Address essential care refusal. Evaluate for depression.
management.biological_interventions: SSRIs for specific/social phobias. Beta-blockers (propranolol) for performance anxiety. Benzodiazepines short-term for exposure sessions.
management.psychological_interventions: Exposure therapy (systematic desensitization, flooding, virtual reality). CBT (cognitive restructuring). Social skills training for social anxiety. Applied relaxation techniques.
management.social_interventions: Gradual exposure support. Family education. Address functional accommodations temporarily. Support groups.
management.follow_up_monitoring: Monitor reduction in fear response. Functional improvement. Assess treatment response.

faculty_pearls: Exposure is the gold standard treatment for phobias - single session can be effective for specific phobias
Virtual reality exposure increasingly available for specific phobias (heights, flying, animals)
Social anxiety involves fear of negative evaluation - CBT focuses on cognitive distortions about scrutiny
Performance anxiety responds well to beta-blockers (propranolol) - reduces somatic symptoms without affecting cognition

assessment.clarify_core: Content of obsessions (contamination, symmetry/ordering, harm (sexual, violent, religious), forbidden thoughts, somatic), frequency, duration, distress (ego-dystonic vs ego-syntonic), attempts to resist/neutralize, time consumed (>1 hr/day?), functional impact
assessment.screen_for_syndrome: OCD: compulsions present or mental acts? Screening for tics (distinguish from compulsions). Depression (common comorbidity). Other anxiety disorders. Psychosis (delusions vs obsessions). Schizotypal (magical thinking).
assessment.rule_out_mimics: Neurological: Tourette's (tics, preceded by premonitory urge), Parkinson's (involuntary movements), basal ganglia disorders. Encephalitis. Substance: stimulants, hallucinogens, amphetamines. Medication: dopamine agonists.
assessment.psychosocial_context: Family OCD history, trauma (sometimes triggers), stress exacerbates, personality traits (perfectionism, high responsibility), religious/cultural factors, learned behaviors
assessment.risk_assessment: Severe distress leading to self-harm/suicide. Harm obsessions (fear of acting on violent/sexual thoughts). Functional impairment. Compulsive behaviors causing physical harm (washing, checking). Substance use to manage distress.

differential_diagnosis.primary_psychiatric: OCD, OCD spectrum disorders (body dysmorphic disorder, hoarding, trichotillomania, excoriation disorder), Depressive disorder with ruminations, GAD (worry), Psychosis (delusions), Schizotypal PD, Tourette's disorder
differential_diagnosis.secondary_mimics: Tourette's syndrome (tics vs compulsions), neurological conditions, stimulant effects, medication side effects, cultural/religious practices
differential_diagnosis.red_flags: Psychotic features (fixed delusions, hallucinations). Harm obsessions with violent thoughts - assess risk. Severe depression with suicidality. Physical harm from compulsions

management.immediate_priorities: Assess for harm risk (to self or others). Evaluate severe distress/suicidality. Address functional impairment.
management.biological_interventions: First-line SSRIs: high dose often needed (fluoxetine, sertraline, paroxetine, fluvoxamine). Clomipramine (TCA) for refractory cases. Antipsychotics (risperidone, haloperidol) as augmentation for refractory OCD. Deep TMS for refractory.
management.psychological_interventions: ERP (Exposure and Response Prevention) - gold standard, first-line. CBT (cognitive restructuring of obsessions). ACT (acceptance-based approach). Habit reversal training.
management.social_interventions: Family education (OCD is brain disorder, not choice). Accommodation reduction (family doesn't help compulsions). Support groups. Address functional impairment.
management.follow_up_monitoring: Monitor obsession/compulsion severity (Y-BOCS). High-dose SSRI trial (10-12 weeks). Consider augmentation if partial response. Long-term management typically needed.

faculty_pearls: Obsessions are ego-dystonic (patient recognizes as unreasonable, distressing) - distinguishes from delusions (ego-syntonic, believed as true)
High-dose, long-duration SSRI trials needed for OCD - often higher than depression doses, 10-12 weeks minimum
ERP (Exposure and Response Prevention) is the gold standard treatment - often more effective than medication alone
Harm obsessions are common in OCD but patients rarely act on them - reassure about ego-dystonic nature

assessment.clarify_core: Specific compulsive behaviors (washing/cleaning, checking, repeating, ordering/arranging, counting, hoarding, mental rituals), premonitory urges (preceding compulsions), relief/neutralization, frequency, duration, time consumed (>1 hr/day?), awareness of excessiveness?, functional impact
assessment.screen_for_syndrome: OCD: obsessions present? (most compulsions in OCD have obsessions, but can be primary). Tourette's: tics (preceded by premonitory urge, can be suppressed temporarily). Body-focused repetitive behaviors (BFRBs: trichotillomania, excoriation, nail-biting). Depression.
assessment.rule_out_mimics: Tourette's syndrome (tics vs compulsions). Neurological: stereotypies in developmental disorders, Parkinson's (repetitive behaviors). Substance: stimulants, amphetamines. Medication: dopamine agonists (levodopa-induced stereotypies).
assessment.psychosocial_context: Family OCD/tic history, stress exacerbates, learned behaviors, personality traits (perfectionism, need for control), reinforcement of compulsions (family accommodation)
assessment.risk_assessment: Physical harm from compulsions (skin damage from washing/excoriation, injury from checking). Functional impairment (time consumed). Self-harm from distress. Depression.

differential_diagnosis.primary_psychiatric: OCD, Tourette's disorder, Body-Focused Repetitive Behaviors (trichotillomania, excoriation disorder), Stereotypic Movement Disorder (in neurodevelopmental disorders), Autism spectrum (stereotypies)
differential_diagnosis.secondary_mimics: Tourette's syndrome, neurological conditions, stimulant effects, medication side effects, cultural/religious practices
differential_diagnosis.red_flags: Psychotic features (compulsive behavior driven by delusions). Severe physical harm (infection, skin breakdown). Complete functional impairment. Depression with suicidality

management.immediate_priorities: Address physical harm from compulsions. Assess for depression/suicidality. Evaluate functional impairment.
management.biological_interventions: For OCD: high-dose SSRIs. For Tourette's: alpha-2 agonists (guanfacine, clonidine), antipsychotics (haloperidol, risperidone). For BFRBs: N-acetylcysteine, SSRIs, habit reversal.
management.psychological_interventions: ERP for OCD. Habit Reversal Training (HRT) for tics/BFRBs. CBT. Behavioral interventions. Response prevention strategies.
management.social_interventions: Family education (reduce accommodation). Address functional consequences. Support groups. Protective measures for harmful compulsions.
management.follow_up_monitoring: Monitor compulsion frequency (Y-BOCS). Assess treatment response. Monitor for physical complications.

faculty_pearls: Distinguish compulsions from tics: compulsions are purposeful (reduce anxiety), tics are semi-voluntary movements with premonitory urge
Family accommodation (helping with compulsions) maintains OCD - reduce accommodation as part of treatment
Habit Reversal Training is effective for tics and BFRBs - awareness, competing response, social support
Physical harm from compulsions (excoriation, washing injuries) requires medical management alongside psychiatric treatment

assessment.clarify_core: Onset, frequency (continuous vs episodic), content (commands, comments, conversations, criticism), location (inside vs outside head), number of voices, loudness, gender familiarity, distress level, control (can ignore?), insight (believes real vs recognizes hallucination)
assessment.screen_for_syndrome: Screen for psychotic disorders: schizophrenia (negative symptoms, disorganization), schizoaffective (mood symptoms + psychosis), brief psychotic disorder, mood disorder with psychotic features. Also assess for mood disorders (bipolar depression, severe mania), PTSD (combat trauma), substance-induced psychosis, neurological conditions.
assessment.rule_out_mimics: Neurological: temporal lobe epilepsy (ictal psychosis), stroke, brain tumors, encephalitis. Substance: alcohol hallucinosis, stimulants (cocaine, amphetamines), hallucinogens (LSD, psilocybin), cannabis (acute), deliriants. Medication: anticholinergics, dopamine agonists (levodopa), antiparkinsonians. Medical: delirium (especially in elderly), severe sensory deprivation, Charles Bonnet syndrome (visual).
assessment.psychosocial_context: Trauma history (combat, assault), family psychosis history, social isolation, migration/urbanicity risk factors, substance use, sleep deprivation, stress
assessment.risk_assessment: Command hallucinations: patient acting on commands? Harm to self/others? Suicidal/homicidal ideation driven by voices. Insight level (protective vs risk). Compliance with safety. History of violence when symptomatic.

differential_diagnosis.primary_psychiatric: Schizophrenia, Schizoaffective Disorder, Brief Psychotic Disorder, Delusional Disorder, Mood Disorder with Psychotic Features (Bipolar, Severe Depression), Substance-Induced Psychotic Disorder
differential_diagnosis.secondary_mimics: Temporal lobe epilepsy, stroke, brain tumors, encephalitis, delirium, substance intoxication/withdrawal, medication side effects, severe sensory deprivation
differential_diagnosis.red_flags: Command hallucinations with dangerous content, poor insight, history of acting on voices, acute onset with focal neurological signs (seizure/stroke), delirium in elderly (medical emergency), catatonia

management.immediate_priorities: Assess danger to self/others from command hallucinations. If high risk: involuntary admission, remove weapons, close observation. Determine insight level. Rule out delirium (medical emergency).
management.biological_interventions: Antipsychotics first-line: second-generation (risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine, aripiprazole, ziprasidone). Consider depot formulation if adherence issues. ECG before/atypical antipsychotics (QTc). MRI/EEG if neurological symptoms or atypical presentation. Treat underlying medical causes.
management.psychological_interventions: CBT for psychosis (normalizing, coping strategies, challenging beliefs about voices). Compliance therapy (medication adherence). Family psychoeducation. Social skills training. Stress management.
management.social_interventions: Family education and support. Supported housing/employment programs. Reduce expressed emotion (family communication). Address social determinants (housing, income).
management.follow_up_monitoring: Monitor psychosis severity (PANSS, BPRS). Monitor antipsychotic side effects (EPS, metabolic, prolactin, QTc). Regular follow-up (weekly to monthly initially). Long-term maintenance typically needed for schizophrenia.

faculty_pearls: Command hallucinations are high-risk - must assess if patient acts on voices
Poor insight in schizophrenia is neurological symptom, not denial or stubbornness - affects adherence
Second-generation antipsychotics better for negative symptoms but higher metabolic risk - monitor weight, glucose, lipids
Family education and reducing expressed emotion significantly improves outcomes and relapse rates

assessment.clarify_core: Content (persecution: being followed, poisoned, harmed; reference: TV talking about them, special messages; grandeur: special powers, divine connection, famous identity), conviction level (fixed vs doubtful), distress, behavior changes (avoidance, safety measures, aggression), insight
assessment.screen_for_syndrome: Screen for psychotic disorders: schizophrenia (other psychotic symptoms, negative symptoms, disorganization), schizoaffective (mood + psychosis), delusional disorder (non-bizarre, mood-congruent possible), mood disorder with psychotic features (bipolar mania, severe depression), brief psychotic disorder. Also consider dementia, delirium.
assessment.rule_out_mimics: Neurological: temporal lobe epilepsy, stroke (especially right parietal), brain tumors, encephalitis. Medical: hypothyroidism (rare), vitamin B12 deficiency, neurosyphilis, HIV, autoimmune encephalitis. Substance: stimulants, cannabis (high potency), hallucinogens, alcohol withdrawal. Medication: corticosteroids, dopamine agonists, anticholinergics. Sensory: Charles Bonnet (visual hallucinations).
assessment.psychosocial_context: Migration/urbanicity, social isolation, trauma, family psychosis history, substance use, cultural factors (some delusions influenced by cultural beliefs)
assessment.risk_assessment: Persecutory delusions → risk of preemptive violence (defensive aggression against perceived persecutor). Command delusions if present. Suicide risk if despair. Self-harm from false beliefs (e.g., removing 'poisoned' limb). Non-compliance with treatment due to delusions.

differential_diagnosis.primary_psychiatric: Schizophrenia, Delusional Disorder, Schizoaffective Disorder, Mood Disorder with Psychotic Features (Bipolar Mania, Severe Depression), Brief Psychotic Disorder, Shared Psychotic Disorder (folie à deux)
differential_diagnosis.secondary_mimics: Temporal lobe epilepsy, stroke, brain tumors, encephalitis, dementia, delirium, substance intoxication/withdrawal, medication side effects, severe sensory deprivation
differential_diagnosis.red_flags: Violence risk from persecutory delusions, catatonia, mood-incongruent delusions (schizoaffective vs schizophrenia), rapid onset (delirium), neurological focal signs, suicidal/homicidal intent from delusional beliefs

assessment.rule_out_mimics: Depression, anxiety disorders, ADHD, PTSD, bipolar depression, sleep deprivation, substance use, hypothyroidism, anemia, vitamin deficiencies, medications (antihistamines, benzos, antiepileptics), neurological conditions (stroke, TBI, dementia).

assessment.clarify_core: Pattern: early morning awakening (with inability to return to sleep), middle-of-night awakenings, difficulty falling asleep (sleep latency >30 min). Duration (>1 month for chronic), frequency (nights/week), bedtime/waketime routines, napping habits, sleep environment, daytime consequences (fatigue, impairment)
assessment.screen_for_syndrome: Depressive symptoms (early morning awakening is hallmark). Anxiety (racing thoughts at bedtime). Mania (decreased sleep need). Substance use (caffeine, alcohol, stimulants). Medical conditions (pain, nocturia, RLS, apnea symptoms). Circadian rhythm disorders.
assessment.rule_out_mimics: Sleep apnea (snoring, witnessed apneas, daytime sleepiness, obesity), RLS (uncomfortable leg sensations relieved by movement), PLMD, circadian rhythm disorders, chronic pain, nocturia (BPH, diabetes), hyperthyroidism, medications (stimulants, steroids, antidepressants), substance use (caffeine, alcohol, nicotine).
assessment.psychosocial_context: Stress/anxiety/worry at bedtime, poor sleep hygiene, irregular schedule, shift work, life stressors, depression, learned insomnia behaviors (conditioned arousal at bedtime)
assessment.risk_assessment: Daytime impairment (driving safety, work errors), fall risk in elderly, depression/suicide, substance use as coping

differential_diagnosis.primary_psychiatric: Insomnia Disorder (psychophysiological, idiopathic), Depressive Disorder, Anxiety Disorders, Circadian Rhythm Disorders, Substance-Induced Sleep Disorder
differential_diagnosis.secondary_mimics: Sleep apnea, RLS/PLMD, circadian rhythm disorders, chronic pain, medical conditions causing sleep disruption, medication side effects
differential_diagnosis.red_flags: Loud snoring + daytime sleepiness + witnessed apneas → OSA (medical, treatable). Sleepwalking/harmful behaviors → parasomnia. Suicidal ideation with early morning awakening.

management.immediate_priorities: Assess for depression/suicide risk (early morning awakening is red flag). Address safety (driving, work errors). Screen for OSA if risk factors.
management.biological_interventions: CBT-I is first-line (not medications). Short-term hypnotics: z-drugs (zolpidem, zopiclone) or benzos (2-4 weeks max). Melatonin for circadian issues. Treat depression/anxiety with SSRIs. Refer for sleep study if OSA suspected.
management.psychological_interventions: CBT for Insomnia (CBT-I): stimulus control, sleep restriction, cognitive restructuring, relaxation techniques. Sleep hygiene education. Worry management.
management.social_interventions: Establish regular sleep schedule. Optimize sleep environment. Address shift work if applicable. Family education.
management.follow_up_monitoring: Monitor sleep diary (sleep latency, efficiency, awakenings). CBT-I response typically 6-8 sessions. Taper hypnotics once CBT effective.

faculty_pearls: CBT-I is more effective long-term than hypnotics and has no dependence risk
Always screen for sleep apnea in chronic insomnia - it's common, dangerous, and treatable
Early morning awakening with inability to return to sleep is hallmark of depression
Hypnotics should be short-term only (2-4 weeks) due to dependence and tolerance risks

assessment.clarify_core: Recent alcohol consumption (amount, timeframe, pattern), timeline of intoxication, symptoms: slurred speech, ataxia, nystagmus, impaired judgment, mood changes (euphoria, dysphoria, aggression), level of consciousness, last drink time, food intake, tolerance history
assessment.screen_for_syndrome: Screen for alcohol use disorder: tolerance, withdrawal, loss of control, use despite harm, cravings, time spent. Also screen for depression, anxiety, psychosis, PTSD, polysubstance use. Assess for complications (liver, pancreatitis, neuropathy).
assessment.rule_out_mimics: Other CNS depressants: benzos, sedatives. Hypoglycemia (diabetic). Stroke (focal deficits, onset timing). TBI (head injury). Hepatic encephalopathy (chronic liver disease). Wernicke's encephalopathy (nystagmus, ataxia, confusion). Other substances: cannabis, opioids.
assessment.psychosocial_context: Drinking context (social, solitary, coping), stressors, family alcohol history, trauma, peer influences, occupation, access to alcohol, cultural factors
assessment.risk_assessment: Acute danger: driving, operating machinery, violence risk, self-harm during intoxication, aspiration risk, falls/trauma, sexual risk (assault vulnerability), withdrawal risk if heavy regular use

differential_diagnosis.primary_psychiatric: Alcohol Intoxication, Alcohol Use Disorder (mild, moderate, severe), Polysubstance Use, Alcohol-Induced Psychotic/Mood/Anxiety Disorder
differential_diagnosis.secondary_mimics: Other CNS depressant intoxication (benzos, sedatives, opioids), hypoglycemia, stroke, TBI, hepatic encephalopathy, Wernicke's encephalopathy, other substance intoxication
differential_diagnosis.red_flags: Wernicke's triad (ataxia, nystagmus, confusion) → medical emergency, thiamine replacement. Coma, respiratory depression, seizures → severe intoxication. Focal neurological signs → consider stroke/TBI.

management.immediate_priorities: Assess level of consciousness, airway protection if needed. Monitor vitals. Check for injuries. Thiamine 100mg IV/IM before glucose if Wernicke's suspected. Ensure safety (observe until sober).
management.biological_interventions: Supportive care for acute intoxication (most cases). Thiamine replacement if suspected deficiency. Treat complications if present. Rule out other causes if atypical presentation. Screen labs: LFTs, CBC, electrolytes.
management.psychological_interventions: Brief intervention/motivational interviewing when sober. Psychoeducation about alcohol use disorder. Relapse prevention planning. CBT for alcohol use.
management.social_interventions: Referral to addiction services. AA/NA groups. Family involvement. Address social determinants. Support services.
management.follow_up_monitoring: Engage with addiction services. Monitor for withdrawal symptoms if heavy use. Screen for alcohol use disorder. Follow-up on complications.

faculty_pearls: Always give thiamine before IV glucose in suspected alcoholics - can precipitate Wernicke's
Brief intervention (motivational interviewing) is effective in acute care settings
Wernicke's encephalopathy is medical emergency - don't miss ataxia + nystagmus + confusion
Assess for alcohol use disorder in intoxication presentations - not just 'drunk', but chronic problem

management.follow_up_monitoring: Monitor mental health (depression, anxiety, suicidality). Monitor hormone effects/safety. Regular follow-up. Long-term supportive care often needed.

Suicide risk is extremely high - assess at every visit, take seriously, have crisis plan
Social transition is medically necessary and not optional for many - support family acceptance
Depression common - often secondary to dysphoria/discrimination, not primary - affirming care reduces risk

assessment.clarify_core: Onset, frequency (passive thoughts vs active daily), content (wish to die, specific plan, methods considered), intent (any intention to act), means (access to lethal methods), past attempts (number, methods, timing), triggers/stressors, protective factors (family, responsibilities, religious/moral objections), current behavior (preparation, goodbyes)
assessment.screen_for_syndrome: Screen for: depression (low mood, anhedonia, hopelessness), bipolarity (mania/mixed episodes, rapid cycling), psychosis (command hallucinations, delusions), PTSD (trauma survivor guilt), borderline personality (emotional lability, abandonment fears), substance use, chronic pain, terminal illness.
assessment.rule_out_mimics: Medical delirium (especially in elderly, post-op), neurological conditions (right hemisphere stroke, tumors), substance intoxication/withdrawal, medication side effects (antidepressants in young adults - activation syndrome).
assessment.psychosocial_context: Recent losses, failures, humiliation, relationship conflicts, family history of suicide, trauma, abuse, bullying, isolation, chronic stress, access to means (firearms, medications), cultural/religious factors
assessment.risk_assessment: IMMEDIATE: Is there current plan? Means access? Intent to act? Past attempts? Protective factors? Risk stratification: low, moderate, high, extreme. Safety: remove means, constant observation, hospitalization if high risk.

differential_diagnosis.primary_psychiatric: Depressive Disorders, Bipolar Disorders (especially during mixed episodes), Schizophrenia, Schizoaffective Disorder, Borderline Personality Disorder, PTSD, Substance Use Disorders
differential_diagnosis.secondary_mimics: Delirium (medical emergency), neurological conditions, substance intoxication/withdrawal, medication side effects, chronic pain, terminal illness
differential_diagnosis.red_flags: Current plan + means + intent → EMERGENCY, hospitalize, constant observation. Command hallucinations. History of attempts (strongest predictor). Severe hopelessness. Mixed episode (high risk). Substance intoxication (poor judgment).

management.immediate_priorities: RISK ASSESSMENT IS NON-NEGOTIABLE. If high/acute risk: involuntary hospitalization, remove means, constant observation, involve family. If moderate risk: safety plan, remove means, close monitoring, follow-up within 24-48 hours. Treat underlying disorder.
management.biological_interventions: Treat underlying disorder: antidepressants for depression, mood stabilizers/antipsychotics for bipolar/psychosis. Consider ECT for severe depression with high suicide risk. Treat agitation with short-term benzos. Monitor closely.
management.psychological_interventions: Crisis intervention, safety planning, CBT for depression/psychosis, DBT for BPD (dialectical approach to suicidal urges), hope-focused interventions, address maladaptive beliefs.
management.social_interventions: Means restriction (firearms, medications). Family involvement and education. Support systems. Address stressors. Safety contracts (with family awareness). Postvention if attempt.
management.follow_up_monitoring: Frequent follow-up initially (daily if high risk, 2-3 days otherwise). Monitor ideation, intent, plan, means, protective factors. Adjust treatment. Long-term management (6-12 months minimum post-crisis).

faculty_pearls: Hopelessness is the strongest predictor of suicide - assess specifically, not just depression severity
Don't be afraid to ask directly about suicide - shows you care and doesn't increase risk
Means restriction works - one of the most effective suicide prevention strategies
Past attempt is strongest risk factor for future suicide - take very seriously
